title: Why Onions Make You Cry: The Chemistry Explained
meta_description: Learn how cutting an onion releases an eye-irritating chemical, why tears follow, and which kitchen techniques can reduce the sting.
author: Suraj Dahal
key_takeaways: Cutting onion cells brings enzymes and sulfur-containing compounds together, leading to formation of the volatile irritant syn-propanethial-S-oxide. [1][2]
The irritant reaches the moist surface of the eye and stimulates sensory nerves, triggering reflex tears that help dilute and wash it away. [1][3]
A sharp knife, gentle cutting and eye protection can reduce exposure; a 2025 study found chilling may increase the tear-triggering droplets released during cutting. [3][4]
The tear response is a protective reflex, not evidence that the onion is poisonous or that the eyes are being permanently damaged by ordinary kitchen exposure. [1][3]

paras: Onions make your eyes water because cutting them releases a volatile sulfur-containing chemical called syn-propanethial-S-oxide, commonly known as the onion lachrymatory factor. When the vapour reaches the surface of your eyes, it irritates sensory endings and triggers the tear glands to produce fluid. The tears dilute and help remove the irritant, which is why your eyes start watering while you chop. [1][2]

The chemistry begins inside the onion. Intact cells keep different compounds separated, but slicing or crushing damages those cells and lets enzymes react with sulfur-containing precursors. One enzyme, lachrymatory-factor synthase, helps produce the tear-inducing compound. This discovery refined earlier explanations that gave the main role to another onion enzyme. The familiar kitchen problem is therefore a small example of plant chemistry and a protective response in the human eye. [1][2]

sections.h2: What happens when an onion is cut
paras: An onion stores sulfur-containing compounds that contribute to its characteristic flavour and smell. In an intact cell, the relevant compounds and enzymes are kept in compartments. A knife breaks the cells open, allowing the materials to mix. Enzymatic reactions transform the precursors through intermediate compounds, and the pathway produces the volatile lachrymatory factor that can travel through the air toward your face. [1][2]

This is why the reaction becomes noticeable during cutting rather than when an onion is simply sitting on the counter. More cell damage can release more of the compounds involved, although the amount also depends on the onion variety, storage and conditions. The vapour does not need to be visible to affect the eyes; many irritating airborne chemicals are detected through their biological effects rather than by sight. [1][2]

sections.h2: Why the eyes respond with tears
paras: The front of the eye is covered by a thin tear film that keeps the surface moist and helps protect it. When an irritant reaches that surface, sensory nerves signal that the eye needs protection. A reflex response increases tear production, spreading fluid across the eye and helping wash away the chemical. The response is automatic, so it can begin before a person consciously thinks about the sting. [1][3]

Reflex tearing is different from emotional crying, even though both produce tears. Emotional tears are linked to brain processes involved in feelings, while onion-induced tears are a protective response to irritation. The eyes may sting, blink more frequently and water heavily, but the symptoms usually ease once exposure stops and the irritant disperses. Persistent pain, vision changes or symptoms that do not settle should not be assumed to be ordinary onion irritation. [3]

sections.h2: Why some onions sting more than others
paras: Onions differ in their sulfur chemistry, growing conditions and variety, so two onions may not produce exactly the same amount of tear-inducing vapour. How the onion is stored and how it is cut can also influence the experience. A cut that crushes many cells may release more reaction products than a clean slice, which is one reason a sharp knife is often recommended. [1][2]

The pungency that makes an onion smell strong is related to its sulfur chemistry, but flavour and eye irritation are not identical measurements. A sweet-tasting onion can still make eyes water, and a strongly flavoured one does not necessarily cause the same reaction in every person. The room’s airflow and the distance between the cutting board and the face also change how much vapour reaches the eyes. [1][2]

A sharp knife and a slower, controlled cutting motion can reduce the spray released as the blade presses through onion layers. A 2025 study reported that the cut can eject tiny droplets at high speed, and that blunt knives and faster chopping released more droplets with greater energy. Cutting gently with a sharpened blade is therefore a practical way to reduce the mist that carries irritants toward the eyes. [3][4]

Protective goggles or a face shield can limit contact between vapour and the eye surface, while good ventilation can help disperse airborne irritants. Avoid rubbing your eyes with onion-contaminated fingers. Chilling onions is often repeated as a tip, but a 2025 report on experimental work found that refrigerated onions produced more tear-triggering droplets when cut; it should not be presented as a dependable prevention method. [3][4][5]

sections.h2: Do onion tears damage your eyes?
paras: For most people, the watering and sting caused by ordinary onion chopping are temporary reflex effects that ease after exposure ends. Tears help dilute and clear the irritant, while blinking spreads the tear film across the surface. The experience can be uncomfortable, but it is not the same as a chemical burn from a strong industrial substance. [1][3]

Still, do not ignore unusual symptoms. Severe or persistent pain, blurred vision, marked redness or symptoms that continue after leaving the kitchen deserve medical advice, especially if another cleaner or chemical may have been involved. If onion juice or residue gets onto the skin or into the eye, rinse gently with clean water and avoid rubbing. The usual onion response should improve as exposure stops. [3]

The chemistry of an onion is part of the way plants manage compounds in their tissues. Sulfur-containing molecules contribute to flavour and aroma, and cell disruption changes which chemicals form and escape. Researchers identified lachrymatory-factor synthase as a key part of the pathway that produces the eye irritant, helping explain why the reaction is not simply a matter of cutting any watery vegetable. [1][2]

The same broad principle appears throughout food preparation: chopping, crushing, heating and mixing change which compounds are released and how they interact. Onion aroma develops from chemical reactions that occur after the tissue is damaged. The tear-inducing reaction is one specific branch of this chemistry, and it explains why a kitchen technique that reduces cell damage can also reduce the amount of vapour reaching the eyes. [1][2]

sections.h2: Common myths and a practical takeaway
paras: A common myth is that onion tears mean the onion is spoiled or unsafe. In fact, the tear-inducing compound is a known product of the onion’s normal chemistry after cells are damaged. Another myth is that one trick works for everyone. Chilling, ventilation and a sharp knife may help, but the result depends on the onion and the conditions in the kitchen. [1][2]

The practical lesson is simple: reduce unnecessary crushing, move the vapour away from your face and avoid touching your eyes while preparing food. If you still tear up, step away briefly and let the irritation settle. The process is a useful reminder that everyday cooking is full of chemistry, and that the body’s automatic responses often protect sensitive surfaces from irritants. [1][3]

faq.q: What chemical makes onions cause tears?
faq.a: The main tear-inducing chemical is syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a volatile lachrymatory factor produced through enzyme-driven reactions after onion cells are damaged. [1][2]

faq.q: Why do onions make you cry but not potatoes?
faq.a: Onions contain sulfur compounds and enzymes that form the lachrymatory factor when their cells are cut. Potatoes do not produce this same reaction pathway. [1][2]

faq.q: Does chilling an onion prevent tears?
faq.a: Not reliably. Although older advice suggests chilling can slow enzyme reactions, a 2025 report on cutting experiments found refrigerated onions produced more tear-triggering droplets. A sharp knife, slow controlled cuts and protective eyewear are better-supported practical choices. [3][4][5]
Ordinary onion-induced tearing is usually temporary. Severe pain, vision changes or symptoms that persist after exposure ends should be assessed rather than assumed to be normal irritation. [1][3]

faq.q: Why do some onions make me cry more?
faq.a: Onion varieties and growing or storage conditions affect their chemistry. Cutting technique and airflow also influence how much irritant reaches the eyes. [1][2]
